articles.title: ‘World’s first’: Ukraine claims heavy-lift drone rescued wounded soldier from frontline
articles.summary: Ukraine has turned a heavy-lift drone into a flying ambulance, lifting a wounded soldier out of a frontline kill zone where mines and Russian drone
articles.body: Ukraine has turned a heavy-lift drone into a flying ambulance, lifting a wounded soldier out of a frontline kill zone where mines and Russian drone activity had made a ground evacuation too dangerous.According to Ukraine’s official military news agency ArmyInform, Ukrainian forces have evacuated a wounded soldier from a frontline position using a heavy-lift hexacopter after Russian drone activity Znd mined terrain made a ground evacuation too dangerous.The operation, carried out using a drone supplied by Ukrainian manufacturer Gurzuf Defence, is being described by Kyiv as the world’s first such evacuation and highlights how aerial drones could offer a new way to rescue troops from heavily contested battlefields.According to The War Zone (TWZ), the operation involved personnel from Ukraine’s 92nd, 30th and 14th Mechanised Brigades, the 10th Army Corps and Gurzuf Defence. The wounded infantryman belonged to the 30th Mechanised Brigade, while a UAV operator from the same formation piloted the heavy-lift hexacopter. The soldier remained in contact with the operator throughout the extraction.TWZ reported that the aircraft was supplied free of charge by Ukrainian manufacturer Gurzuf Defence. Military specialists worked with the company to adapt the drone for the mission, with the technical solution designed to keep the aircraft stable and prevent excessive swaying or tipping during flight.The footage shows the soldier securing himself beneath the hexacopter with a harness before being lifted into the air. Unlike a conventional medical evacuation helicopter, the drone carried him suspended beneath its frame, without an enclosed cabin or a protected medical compartment.The military said the soldier was rescued successfully and was undergoing treatment and rehabilitation, with his life no longer in danger.Ukraine has increasingly relied on unmanned ground vehicles to deliver supplies and evacuate casualties from exposed positions. However, mines, mud and cratered terrain can prevent ground robots from reaching wounded troops, while hostile drones and artillery make movement through frontline areas dangerous.An aerial platform offers a potential alternative by bypassing ground obstacles and reaching positions inaccessible to ground vehicles.Why this is a big dealThe operation highlights a potential shift in how wounded soldiers could be evacuated from modern battlefields, where drones, landmines and artillery make conventional rescue missions increasingly dangerous.The approach could also expand the role of heavy-lift drones beyond carrying supplies and equipment. If successfully developed for repeated frontline use, these platforms could provide military commanders with another option for recovering injured troops from positions inaccessible to ground vehicles.However, the method has significant limitations. The footage shows the soldier suspended beneath the aircraft, leaving him exposed during flight. The harness-based approach could also prove difficult for unconscious personnel or those too severely injured to secure themselves. The aircraft’s range, endurance and ability to operate reliably under enemy fire remain unclear.

articles.title: An energy company is giving Yellowstone National Park a record $105 million gift; the money will fund conservation, student trips and a new visitor centre
articles.summary: Yellowstone National Park, the world’s first national park, is set to receive a $105 million private gift from energy infrastructure company Tallgrass,
articles.body: Yellowstone National Park, the world’s first national park, is set to receive a $105 million private gift from energy infrastructure company Tallgrass, marking the largest single private contribution in the history of the US National Park Service. Announced on October 19, 2026, the funding will establish a permanent Conservation and Stewardship Fund to support scientific research, improve visitor facilities and give more students and community members opportunities to experience the iconic American wilderness. The initiative brings together the National Park Service, Yellowstone Forever, the park’s official nonprofit partner, and Tallgrass, a portfolio company of Blackstone Infrastructure. The money will be directed towards three priorities, including a new visitor centre at Norris Geyser Basin and long-term programmes to expand access to the park for Wyoming students and families.Yellowstone’s record $105 million gift: Where the money will goThe fund will support three major areas: conservation and research, infrastructure improvements and expanded public access. According to the National Park Service, the aim is to establish a lasting source of funding for Yellowstone’s long-term stewardship rather than simply finance a single project.The investment is expected to strengthen the park’s scientific work, improve facilities for visitors and create more opportunities for people living in Wyoming to explore its landscapes and learn about its wildlife.The partnership also reflects an effort to bring private philanthropy into the long-term management and preservation of one of America’s most recognisable natural landmarks. Yellowstone Forever will work alongside the National Park Service and Tallgrass to support the initiative.$50 million for conservation and scientific researchThe largest share of the fund, $50 million, is earmarked for conservation and research. The investment is intended to extend the reach of Yellowstone’s scientific programmes and support work that helps researchers understand and protect the park’s natural resources.Yellowstone is known for its geothermal features, extensive forests, rivers and diverse wildlife. Its ecosystem supports species including bison, elk, wolves and grizzly bears, making research and conservation central to the park’s long-term management.The funding will help sustain scientific work and conservation priorities over time. By establishing a permanent source of support, the initiative aims to provide a longer-term foundation for research and stewardship activities.A new $35 million visitor centre at Norris Geyser BasinAnother $35 million is earmarked for a new visitor education centre at Norris Geyser Basin, one of Yellowstone’s prominent geothermal areas.The basin is known for its hot springs, geysers and other hydrothermal features. The planned centre is intended to improve the visitor experience and provide more opportunities for people to understand the area's distinctive geology and natural environment.The investment will form part of the wider effort to strengthen the park’s infrastructure. Alongside conservation work, improvements to visitor facilities are expected to help people engage with Yellowstone’s natural features and educational resources.The project is one of the clearest examples of how the new fund will translate into a specific development within the park.$20 million to help students and families visit YellowstoneThe remaining $20 million will support a long-term funding pool designed to expand opportunities for students and community members in Wyoming to experience Yellowstone.The initiative will include the Tallgrass WYld Yellowstone Initiative, named after the energy infrastructure company. It is intended to help more young people and families connect with the park through educational and visitor experiences.Access to a national park can provide students with opportunities to learn about wildlife, ecosystems, geology and conservation beyond the classroom. The programme aims to strengthen those opportunities for communities across Wyoming and encourage a lasting connection with the natural environment.The funding is designed to provide continuing support rather than limit the effort to a one-time round of visits.Who is funding Yellowstone’s historic gift?Tallgrass is an energy infrastructure company that has operated in Wyoming for more than a decade. It is part of Blackstone Infrastructure’s portfolio, linking the donation to the investment firm’s infrastructure business.The company said its connection to Wyoming was an important part of the initiative. Its contribution will support a combination of scientific research, visitor infrastructure and educational opportunities, extending beyond a conventional donation to a single conservation project.Blackstone has also framed the investment as a commitment to protecting Yellowstone for future generations. The park’s nonprofit partner, Yellowstone Forever, supports research, restoration and educational experiences, making it a central partner in the new fund.The announcement brings private funding, conservation expertise and public park management together around a shared long-term objective.National Park Service will retain control over park managementDespite the scale of the donation, the National Park Service will retain full authority over decisions concerning Yellowstone’s management. Projects funded through the initiative must comply with applicable laws, policies and park priorities.The arrangement places the money within a framework intended to support the park’s existing responsibilities rather than replace public oversight.Yellowstone was established in 1872 and spans approximately 2.2 million acres across Wyoming, Montana and Idaho. Its geothermal landscapes and wildlife have made it one of the United States’ best-known protected areas.The $105 million fund is intended to provide sustained support for the park’s scientific work, facilities and educational access. By combining conservation research with improvements for visitors and opportunities for students, the initiative aims to strengthen Yellowstone’s protection and public value for generations to come.You use AI every day. articles.body: Opposition spending against California’s first-of-its-kind wealth tax referendum, known as Proposition 40, has surged past $1 million a day, a report has said, adding that the massive financial push appears to be shifting public opinion as the latest polling data revealing that the proposed measure is losing momentum rapidly as the November 3 election approaches. If passed, Proposition 40 would levy a one-time 5% tax on individuals with net worths exceeding $1 billion, assessing their assets and unrealised capital gains. Approximately 90% of the generated revenue would go toward funding public healthcare services to offset federal funding shortfalls.However, the initiative has triggered resistance from corporate leaders, Silicon Valley tech royalty, and Democratic Governor Gavin Newsom, a recent report by Frobes said. Opponents argue that merely advancing the proposal is accelerating an exodus of high-net-worth residents, threatening long-term damage to the state's revenue base and broader economy.Data shows reversal ahead of November 3 polling dayRecent polling indicates that as opposition advertising intensifies, voter enthusiasm for the ballot measure is eroding sharply. From August to Mid-September, the report claimed, six independent surveys showed California voters leaning toward a “yes” vote, leading by margins ranging from 2% to 10%. In late September, a survey by the Independent Voter Project showed the momentum had flipped, with the “no” opposition taking a 4-point lead.Citing a latest poll, the report said that a survey released by the Manhattan Institute shows the “no” vote pulling ahead by a substantial 15-point margin.Campaign spending data highlights a staggering financial imbalance between the two camps. According to reporting from The Guardian, the opposition effort has assembled more than $340 million, burning through upwards of $1 million per day during the first half of September alone.Dave Regan, head of California's largest healthcare workers' union, which is the primary sponsor of Proposition 40, told The New York Times Magazine that he expects opposition groups to spend at least $400 million by the November 3 vote.By contrast, the healthcare workers' union backing the tax has raised $32 million, which is less than 10% of the opposition's total resources.Top donors funding the fight against Proposition 40A prominent group of technology founders, venture capitalists, and executives has financed the opposition campaign. articles.title: 'They chose Canada': Alberta rejects separation bid in win for Carney
articles.summary: Voters in Canada's oil-rich Alberta province have overwhelmingly rejected a move towards independence.
articles.body: Voters in Canada's oil-rich Alberta province have overwhelmingly rejected a move towards independence. They delivered a boost to Prime Minister Mark Carney's push for national unity amid US President Donald Trump's trade war and threats to annex Canada.With more than 1.5 million votes counted, 76 per cent backed remaining in Canada, while nearly 24 per cent supported beginning the process towards separation, according to unofficial results from Elections Alberta on Tuesday. The referendum was not a direct vote on independence. Approval would have paved the way for a future vote on separation.“Albertans made a clear choice,” Carney said, “They chose unity, to build together, and to take care of each other. Above all, Albertans chose Canada,” news agency AFP reported.Carney said the result would allow the country to move forward together. He also called for faster efforts to diversify trade, develop major infrastructure projects and establish Canada as a global energy powerhouse, with Alberta at its centre.Alberta Premier Danielle Smith also welcomed the early results, saying they reflected support for the province remaining within Canada.“Albertans have voted for a stronger Alberta in a united Canada,” Smith posted on social media.Smith had called the referendum amid growing pressure from separatists within her governing United Conservative Party (UCP), despite opposing independence. She was due to address the province on Tuesday evening about the results and Alberta's future.The results were delayed after late openings forced more than 100 polling stations to extend voting hours on Monday.Separatists vow to continue campaignDespite the apparent setback, separatist leaders said the movement had gained ground and would continue to push for independence.“We don't have the final results. I think the numbers are going to fluctuate, but it is fair to say that at least a quarter of Albertans feel that Alberta needs to be treated better,” said Keith Wilson, a leader of the separatist movement.At a referendum night gathering in an Edmonton restaurant, supporters fell silent as the results came in. Jeff Rath of the Alberta Prosperity Project said the campaign had succeeded in bringing the issue into public debate.“We're not going anywhere,” he said. “We've dominated the conversation in the last year. We've been educating Albertans on the benefits of independence, and we're going to continue moving forward.”Rath had said he would be thrilled if 30 per cent of voters backed beginning the separation process. He also called for Smith to be ousted as UCP leader, warning that the party could split and potentially give rise to a new pro-independence party.However, Thomas Lukaszuk, a former Alberta deputy premier who led the Forever Canadian campaign against separation, welcomed the outcome.“We are a solid country that's united from coast to coast to coast,” he told supporters.Trump's threats strengthen push for unityAlberta is home to the world's fourth-largest proven oil reserves. The province is also a conservative stronghold whose political culture has long had more in common with the American West than much of Canada.Resentment towards the federal government in Ottawa runs deep, but it has not traditionally translated into widespread support for independence. Separatist parties previously attracted only 1 per cent or 2 per cent of the vote, former premier Jason Kenney said.Anger over Covid-19 restrictions helped mobilise activists who later embraced the separatist cause, Kenney said. Trump's trade war and threats to make Canada the 51st US state have since helped Carney rally support in Alberta, where Liberal prime ministers have historically been unpopular.Carney had urged voters to deliver a decisive mandate for unity ahead of the referendum.“Vote like Canada's future depends on it, because it does,” he told a rally in Edmonton on Friday. The city is where he grew up.The vote also exposed the divide between separatist sentiment and concerns about the cost of living and public services.Dustin Degenhardt, a voter in Wainwright, said Alberta had long been mistreated by the federal government.“Alberta has essentially been treated as, you know, a colony,” he said after voting on Monday. “They want to take and take and take from us, and not return anything.”Dave Malka, 59, of Edmonton, questioned the decision to spend money on what he called a “referendum on a referendum” instead of healthcare.With Trump threatening Canada, Malka said, “It seems to be happening at the absolute worst time when we should be united; instead we're fighting among ourselves.”You use AI every day. articles.title: What Does Your Moon Sign Reveal About How You React When Someone Hurts You?
articles.summary: Two people hear the same harsh remark at a family dinner. One snaps back on the spot.
articles.body: Two people hear the same harsh remark at a family dinner. One snaps back on the spot. The other smiles, finishes the meal and doesn’t speak to that relative for a year. Astrology often traces this difference to the Moon sign. The Sun shows who a person is trying to become. The Moon shows how they feel, especially when they are caught off guard. Because the Moon changes sign about every two and a half days, you need an accurate birth date and time to find it. In Vedic astrology, this placement is called the Rashi.Fire Moons: Aries, Leo and SagittariusMoon in Aries reacts fast. The hurt turns into anger within seconds, and words come out before thought catches up. But the storm passes just as quickly. By the next morning, an Aries Moon may have forgotten the fight while the other person is still upset.Moon in Leo takes hurt as an insult to its dignity. These natives may go quiet and cold, waiting for an apology that properly acknowledges their feelings. A casual “sorry, yaar” often isn’t enough. They need to feel that the other person understands what was damaged.Moon in Sagittarius often tries to laugh it off. A joke covers the sting. If the hurt runs deep, they may simply leave, either by planning a trip or by spending long hours outside the house. Distance is how they cool down.Earth Moons: Taurus, Virgo and CapricornThe Moon is exalted in Taurus, so Moon in Taurus is usually calm and steady. It takes a lot to upset them. Once hurt, though, they hold on. They may not argue. They just stop trusting, and getting that trust back takes patience and consistent effort.Moon in Virgo analyses the hurt. These natives replay the conversation, looking for what went wrong and sometimes blaming themselves. A sleepless night spent rereading old messages is common. Practical apologies work best, especially ones that include a clear change in behaviour.Moon in Capricorn hides its pain behind work. After a betrayal, a Capricorn Moon may suddenly put in extra hours at the office. They rarely cry in front of others. The hurt shows later, in quiet withdrawal from the person who caused it.Air Moons: Gemini, Libra and AquariusMoon in Gemini wants to talk it out, sometimes with everyone except the person involved. Calling two friends and having a long chat with a sibling helps them process. They can also rationalise the pain too quickly and skip over feelings that need more time.Moon in Libra avoids open conflict. These natives may smile and say “it’s fine” when it clearly isn’t. Their hurt comes out later, often in small comments. A gentle, private conversation in a calm setting helps them say what they actually feel.Moon in Aquarius detaches. They stand back and see the situation from an outsider’s perspective. People sometimes mistake this for coldness. Underneath, the hurt is real, and it often relates to feeling excluded or misunderstood.Water Moons: Cancer, Scorpio and PiscesThe Moon rules Cancer, which makes the Moon in Cancer deeply sensitive. Old memories mix with new pain, so a small slight can bring back years of hurt. They may retreat into home and family, needing reassurance before they open up again.The Moon is debilitated in Scorpio, and the Moon in Scorpio feels hurt intensely. These natives rarely forget. Some test the person who hurt them before deciding whether to forgive. Others cut contact silently. Either way, the response is never casual.Moon in Pisces absorbs the hurt and often forgives too soon. They can find reasons to excuse the other person, even when the behaviour repeats. Setting limits doesn’t come naturally, yet this placement often teaches it.Knowing each Moon sign's natural reaction helps. It gives a moment to pause before the familiar pattern takes over.Get the latest astrology news and horoscope updates. Download the TOI App.

articles.title: The backstory: When West 'tricked' Russia to overthrow Muammar Gaddafi's regime in Libya
articles.summary: Fifteen years ago, Muammar Gaddafi’s over four-decade-long dictatorial rule in Libya ended in a drainage pipe.
articles.body: Fifteen years ago, Muammar Gaddafi’s over four-decade-long dictatorial rule in Libya ended in a drainage pipe. A Nato raid had struck his convoy, and insurgents executed him while Western capitals cheered."We came, we saw, he died," Hillary Clinton, then US secretary of state, famously quipped. Moscow watched with a very different feeling. Many Russians, primarily Vladimir Putin, were convinced they had been played.Gaddafi's regime fell during the Arab Spring, the wave of uprisings that swept the Middle East and North Africa that year, and his end marked the success of a Western-led military campaign.For Russia, however, it marked something else. Moscow believed it was misled into allowing that campaign, and the resentment still shapes its dealings with the West.The UN resolution 1973The beginning of the end of Gaddafi's regime began at the UN security council, where Russia, the United States, Britain, France and China can each block a decision with a veto. However, the regime's fate in Tripoli was sealed with a trick.On March 17, 2011, with Gaddafi’s forces turning their guns on rebels in Benghazi, the council voted on Resolution 1973. It allowed Nato countries to use "all necessary measures" to protect civilians and banned flights over Libya, while ruling out any foreign occupation force.Russia could have vetoed it, but it chose to abstain, as personally ordered by President Dmitry Medvedev. Moscow failed to read between the lines. And the resolution passed.Nevertheless, UN ambassador, Vitaly Churkin, still warned that the wording allowed wide-ranging military intervention. But it all fell on deaf ears.Kremlin had read the resolution as a shield for civilians, starting with the city of Benghazi, plus a ban on flights over Libya.The resolution did rule out a foreign occupation force, which sounded like a limit, but that limit covered only a land invasion. For everything else, the text authorised "all necessary measures" to protect civilians under threat, and it never specified who would judge what was necessary.Western powers, basically, maintained that civilians would remain at risk as long as Gaddafi was in power. The objective was clear. Regime change.A year later, a Western diplomat involved with the resolution said he was "astonished" that the Russians had allowed it. "We would have settled for much less," he told journalist Jeremy Bowen.When Putin felt playedAfter the US, France and Britain launched airstrikes against Libya, Russia accused them of exceeding the mandate granted by Resolution 1973. Moscow believed the authorisation to protect civilians had become a means of removing Gaddafi from power, allowing Western governments to reshape Libya’s political future at Russia’s expense.Vladimir Putin, then Russia’s prime minister, condemned the resolution by comparing it to a medieval call for a crusade. He believed that Gaddafi had forfeited his legitimacy by ordering violence against civilians, but warned that a military overthrow could plunge Libya into prolonged instability.Russia subsequently explored a diplomatic solution through its envoy, Mikhail Margelov. Margelov maintained that political crises could not be resolved through military force alone. Despite these efforts, Moscow failed to halt the campaign led by Nato, which also received support from wealthy regional allies, including Qatar.The lesson Moscow took to SyriaSergey Lavrov, who served as Russia’s ambassador to the UN during the 1999 Kosovo crisis, viewed the Libya intervention as another instance in which Western powers had exploited a Security Council resolution to advance their own objectives. Western officials believed the experience reinforced his determination to prevent a similar outcome in Syria.When the Syrian conflict came before the security council, Russia and China repeatedly blocked efforts to condemn President Bashar al-Assad’s government. Moscow would eventually exercise its veto on Syria 15 more times. Libyan episode also weakened Dmitry Medvedev’s influence over Russian foreign policy while strengthening hardliners within the defence ministry.Russia, therefore, continues to blame Nato for Libya’s collapse, arguing that the intervention undermined state institutions and contributed to the spread of terrorism and migration. Nato maintains that its operation was legitimate and necessary, while attributing Libya’s subsequent crisis to developments from 2014 onwards.Whether Moscow misjudged the resolution’s language or believed Western powers had deliberately exploited it remains contested. However, the intervention left Russia deeply distrustful of Western-backed resolutions and more determined to prevent similar outcomes in subsequent conflicts.You use AI every day. articles.title: Billionaire Mark Cuban set up a ‘chain letter’ to pay his fees in junior year of college; he now admits it was basically Ponzi scheme, here’s how it worked
articles.summary: Mark Cuban relied on unconventional college hustles just to stay enrolled.
articles.body: Mark Cuban relied on unconventional college hustles just to stay enrolled. Long before rising to fame as a celebrity investor on Shark Tank, owning the NBA’s Dallas Mavericks and joining the ranks of the world’s wealthiest individuals, Cuban ran a ‘Ponzi’ scheme. Speaking on the San Francisco Standard podcast recently, the 68-year-old billionaire entrepreneur opened up about how he financed his junior year of college at Indiana University in the early 1980s: by launching a dorm room "chain letter" that he now candidly admits operated as a ‘scam’.“It was basically a scam. I made sure my friends all got their money back. And so I got up to the top of the list. And it was amazing, because I’d go to [my mailbox] and there’d be envelopes with 50 bucks from here, 50 bucks from there, and that’s how I paid for my junior year of college,” Cuban admitted with a chuckle during the podcast appearance.How the dorm room ‘Chain Letter’ workedFaced with mounting educational costs, Cuban kicked off the network by approaching an initial participant and asking for $100 upfront, structuring an informal financial pyramid:Cuban collected $100, pocketed $50 immediately and directed the remaining $50 to the dorm resident whose name sat at the top of a 10-person list.The top name was removed, and the new payer’s name was added at the bottom, creating a $50 circulating chain letter.As successive students paid in and recruited others, names moved higher on the list until participants reached the top slot, theoretically collecting cash from incoming buyers.Cuban pitched the scheme as a way for participants to walk away with more cash than they put in. As the chain expanded through the dorms, envelopes stuffed with $50 contributions began arriving steadily at his mailbox, covering his college tuition and living expenses for the year.Mark Cuban: From trash bags to techFinding resourceful ways to earn cash was nothing new for Cuban, who was raised in a working-class household in suburban Pittsburgh. His father, who worked in automotive upholstery, occasionally handed him a $20 bill, but taught him early on to fund his own desires. When a young Cuban asked his father for a new pair of basketball shoes, his father replied that once he had a job, he could purchase whatever he wanted.That conversation launched Cuban’s sales career at an early age. Taking advantage of an opportunity through a family friend who had surplus boxes of trash bags, Cuban began knocking on doors throughout his neighborhood to sell household supplies.“I would go door-to-door to be like, ‘Hi, my name is Mark. Do you use trash bags?’ I killed it.” Cuban recalled.After graduating from college, Cuban relocated to Dallas, where he shared a cramped apartment, which he and his roommates dubbed a “hell hotel”, with five other young men.Cuban slept on the floor, took a bed only when a roommate went out of town, and owned neither a closet nor a dresser. To make ends meet, he worked as a software salesman while spending his spare time reading tech manuals to master computer programming and operating systems.You use AI every day. articles.title: In 1851-52, a Delhi artist painted the only known portrait of Bahadur Shah Zafar's spiritual adviser Kale Miyan; the rare image reached the US art market in 2000 and sold in London for £63,500 in 2026
articles.summary: In the final years of Mughal rule in Delhi, an artist painted a portrait of Ghulam Nasir al-Din, a spiritual adviser to Emperor Bahadur Shah Zafar.
articles.body: In the final years of Mughal rule in Delhi, an artist painted a portrait of Ghulam Nasir al-Din, a spiritual adviser to Emperor Bahadur Shah Zafar. Known as Kale Miyan, he was a respected religious figure whose influence extended to the imperial court. The painting, dated 1851-52, is now considered the only known portrait of him. After appearing on the American art market in 2000, the rare work sold at Christie's in London for £63,500 on April 28, 2026.According to the official website of British auction house Christie's, the painting was created in Mughal Delhi by a follower of Ghulam Ali Khan, regarded as one of the foremost painters of 19th-century Delhi. The work was offered as part of The Mary and Cheney Cowles Collection of Indian Painting and Calligraphy. The auction house estimated it at £30,000 to £50,000. The final price of £63,500 exceeded the upper estimate by £13,500.A portrait from the last years of the Mughal courtThe painting depicts Kale Miyan seated between two attendants in a formal setting. Made with opaque pigments heightened with gold on paper and laid down on card, it measures approximately 23 by 33.8 cm. A halo-like nimbus around the central figure draws attention to his religious standing, while his relatively simple clothing reflects his spiritual identity. According to Christie's website, the subject is identified as Ghulam Nasir al-Din, also known as Miyan Kali Sahib Qibla. An inscription on the painting describes it as the “Blessed likeness of His Excellence Ghulam Nasir al-Din known as Miyan Kali Sahib Qibla” and gives the date as 1268 in the Hijri calendar, corresponding to 1851-52.The painting also identifies two members of his family and spiritual lineage: his father, Qutb al-Din, and his grandfather, Fakhr al-Din. According to Christie's, their names appear in the inscriptions, highlighting the religious lineage associated with Kale Miyan. The auction house notes that Kale Miyan's family traced its lineage to Nizam al-Din, whose shrine was in Aurangabad. His grandfather Fakhr al-Din moved to Delhi in the mid-18th century, and his father Qutb al-Din succeeded him.Kale Miyan served as the ‘murshid,’ or spiritual guide, to Bahadur Shah Zafar, the last Mughal emperor, who ruled from 1837 to 1857. The portrait was made only a few years before the Indian Rebellion of 1857, which brought Mughal rule in Delhi to an end.The man known as Kale MiyanThe nickname Kale Miyan means “The Black Gentleman” and referred to his dark complexion, according to Christie's. His reputation was closely tied to his spiritual role rather than the display of wealth or imperial power. As per the auction catalogue, Thomas Beale's ‘Oriental Biographical Dictionary of British India,’ published in 1895, stated that Ghulam Nasir al-Din always “preferred the habit of a dervish”. The painting's simple clothing and religious halo are consistent with the spiritual identity described in the catalogue. Bahadur Shah Zafar's relationship with his spiritual adviser remained significant even after the collapse of the Mughal court. Following the 1857 uprising, the British exiled the emperor to Yangon, then known as Rangoon, in present-day Myanmar.According to the Christie's catalogue, Zafar asked his captors for the privilege of being buried alongside his spiritual guide. That request was not granted. The circumstances of Kale Miyan's death remain uncertain. Some accounts place his death in 1852, while the poet Mirza Ghalib, who knew him, claimed that the British killed him during the siege of Delhi. Ghalib also recorded the destruction of Kale Miyan's ancestral home, describing it as though a broom had swept it away, leaving no scrap of paper, thread of gold or yarn of wool. The conflicting accounts underline how much of the history surrounding Kale Miyan remains difficult to establish.The artist behind the rare imageChristie's attributes the painting to a follower of Ghulam Ali Khan, whose career spanned the first half of the 19th century. Although the artist behind this particular work is not identified by name, the auction house says the painting carries the hallmark style of the Delhi painter's school. Ghulam Ali Khan worked for both Indian and European patrons. He began as a topographical artist before turning to portraiture and is associated with works documenting people, places and court life in northern India. He also worked at regional courts, including those of Alwar, Jhajjar and Dujana.A second drawing on the reverseThe artwork has another detail that is easy to overlook. As per Christie's website, the reverse of the sheet carries a pen-and-ink drawing of boats moored by Patna. The portrait and the drawing on its reverse bring together two different kinds of visual record on the same sheet: a carefully composed image of a prominent religious figure and a scene of boats along a riverfront.The painting's documented ownership history is relatively brief. Christie's lists its provenance as the American art market in 2000, before it entered the collection offered in London in 2026.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: Between 1723 and 1735, Qing artisans made a porcelain bowl painted with bats and peaches; after passing through a Paris dealer and spending 87 years at a Chicago museum, it sold for $2.048 million in New York
articles.summary: A rare porcelain bowl made by skilled imperial craftsmen during China's Qing dynasty in the early 18th century has sold for $2.048 million (£1.56 million)
articles.body: A rare porcelain bowl made by skilled imperial craftsmen during China's Qing dynasty in the early 18th century has sold for $2.048 million (£1.56 million) at a Christie's auction in New York. The 14.3-centimetre bowl was made during the short reign of Emperor Yongzheng, which lasted from 1723 to 1735. In the early 20th century, it passed through the hands of a well-known Paris art dealer. It was later bought by a private collector and donated to the Art Institute of Chicago in 1939. The bowl remained in the museum's collection for 87 years before being put up for auction to raise money for the care and growth of its Asian art collection. According to a press statement from Christie's, the final sale price was five times the bowl's lowest pre-sale estimate. The sale was part of a major two-day autumn auction series in New York, which brought in a total of $25.96 million (£19.8 million) from Chinese works of art.Imperial craftsmanship and artistic techniqueThe bowl is an example of famille rose porcelain, a style of coloured enamel decoration that was developed to a high level during the Qing dynasty. According to catalogue notes published by Christie's, the bowl uses a design method known as guozhihua, or "flowering branch passing over the rim". In this technique, the painted design starts on the outside of the bowl and continues over its rim onto the inside. Creating guozhihua designs on curved porcelain bowls was very difficult for imperial craftsmen because they had only a small, rounded surface to work on. To make the peaches look realistic, the artisans blew fine enamel powders directly onto the glazed ceramic. They then used brushes to add details and create smooth colour changes from pale green to rose pink. The design features six ripe peaches and five red bats shown flying across both the outside and inside of the bowl.Auspicious symbolism and imperial contextIn traditional Chinese imperial art, each image has a deeper meaning. According to Christie's description of the auction lot, the combination of six peaches and five red bats suggests that the bowl may have been made for Emperor Yongzheng's birthday.In Chinese art and symbolism:Peaches stand for long life. They are linked to the Daoist star god Shou Lao and the legendary orchards of the Queen Mother of the West.The number six, or liu, is linked to the idea of keeping or extending a long life.Five red bats, known as hong fu, represent the Five Blessings: health, long life, wealth, love of virtue and a peaceful death.The phrase guoqiangzhi, meaning "branch passing over the wall", sounds like guo chang zhi, which translates as "long peace under good government".Because these symbols carry several connected meanings, historians and ceramics experts consider bowls with this combination of designs to be among the finest examples of porcelain made for the Yongzheng court.Ownership history and auction performanceBefore joining the Art Institute of Chicago's collection, the bowl belonged to C.T. Loo (1880–1957), a leading Chinese art dealer who worked in Paris during the early 20th century. It was later bought by Russell Tyson (1867–1963), a Chicago art collector and supporter of the museum. Tyson donated the bowl to the Art Institute of Chicago, where it was officially added to the permanent collection in 1939. The bowl was offered as a leading item in Christie's sale titled Important Chinese Art Including Ceramics from the Art Institute of Chicago. Vicki Paloympis, head of the Chinese Ceramics and Works of Art Department at Christie's in New York, spoke about strong demand for imperial artworks with a clear record of ownership. "This season we had two fantastic sales that showed great results," Paloympis said in a statement released by Christie's. "As we have seen in previous seasons, but now more than ever, the strongest results were driven by works that combined superb quality with exceptional provenance." Paloympis added that the strong interest in items from the Art Institute of Chicago showed that buyers place great value on artworks with well-documented ownership histories. The Art Institute of Chicago will keep the $2.048 million raised from the sale to support future purchases and preservation work across its Asian art department.You use AI every day. articles.title: Is Russia stalking satellites which help Ukraine from space?
articles.summary: Analysts say a Russian craft’s close pass by a commercial radar satellite is a first and a warning to Kyiv’s backers.
articles.body:
A Russian military satellite has manoeuvred to within metres of a US-registered radar satellite believed to provide intelligence to Ukraine, according to space-tracking data reported by The War Zone, a US defence news site.

Cosmos 2612 may have passed ICEYE-X36, a satellite owned by the US arm of the Finnish company ICEYE.

LeoLabs, a US space-tracking company, put the closest approach at about 500 metres, according to Breaking Defence.

ICEYE has supplied radar imagery to Ukraine since 2022, Defence News reported.

So is Russia stalking satellites which help Ukraine from space? Al Jazeera spoke to analysts to find out:

A Russian satellite has deliberately positioned itself close to a Western one, after months of manoeuvring.

Cosmos 2612 is one of six satellites the Russian military launched in April, The War Zone reported.

In May, four of them moved close to an ICEYE satellite.

ICEYE-X36 is a commercial satellite, owned by a private company rather than a government, but ICEYE sells radar imagery to militaries and supplies data to the US and its allies.

ICEYE’s chief executive, Rafal Modrzewski, told the Reuters news agency the company then moved its own satellite, which appeared to prompt further Russian manoeuvres.

Then, between Thursday and Friday last week, Cosmos 2612 closed in from more than 320km (200 miles) from ICEYE-X36 to about 4.8km (3 miles), the space-tracking company LeoLabs told the news site Axios.

Over the weekend, it moved between positions ahead of and behind the ICEYE satellite, at times coming within roughly 500 metres, LeoLabs said in a report on Monday, adding that the estimate was uncertain and, by Monday, it had begun to move away.

A Ukrainian official told Axios that Ukraine’s military works with ICEYE and uses its capabilities, but said it was unclear whether ICEYE-X36 itself supports Ukraine.

Has Russia done this before, and what is the purpose?

In the past, Russia has mainly carried out such manoeuvres against Western military satellites, rather than commercially owned ones, Mark Hilborne, a senior lecturer in the defence studies department at King’s College London, told Al Jazeera.

In early 2020, two Russian satellites moved close to USA 245, a US spy satellite.

In September 2025, German Defence Minister Boris Pistorius said two Russian Luch-Olymp satellites were tracking two Intelsat satellites used by the German military.

Dr Marco Langbroek, a lecturer in optical space situational awareness at TU Delft Faculty of Aerospace Engineering, said: “At geostationary altitude, we have seen two Russian satellites (LUCH/OLYMP-K 1 & 2) repeatedly approach western communication satellites to distances of a few tens of kilometres in the past few years, likely with the intention to eavesdrop on communications and data transfers. And we have seen the Russians practising very close approaches in Low Earth Orbit – similar to what they now did to ICEYE-X36 – with their own satellites as test targets.”

However, this incident is different, because “approaching another satellite this close without the cooperation of the owner or operator of the other satellite, is widely considered ‘not done’ as it is dangerous, with a risk of collision or interference.

“It is equivalent to placing your car on the freeway within 10 cm of another driving car: highly unsafe.”

Langbroek said it is not known what the purpose of the Russian manoeuvre was, however, “it could be a dry run for a future attack, it could be provocation or scare tactics to ruffle the feathers of Ukraine and its allies, and/or a test to see how the satellite operators react to a threat like this.”

This sort of manoeuvre, therefore, falls into the pattern of “hybrid warfare” – “the same kind of provocations and inciting reactions like what Russia does when they fly a drone into Polish airspace or zoom a NATO warship at low elevation in the Baltic Sea”.

Close approaches have happened for years, but not like this.

Hilborne said this is “the first time that a country has done such a manoeuvre … against the commercial satellite without any consent”.

It was also “incredibly close”, he said, with some reports putting the distance at less than 30 metres.

Far more common is interference that does not require going near a satellite at all. This is mostly done through jamming, which drowns out a satellite’s signals, often from the ground.

Western military officials told Reuters that Russian interference with Western space systems has increased significantly since its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.

For Hilborne, the choice of target “is starting to indicate that Russia does not distinguish between commercial and military satellites as potential targets”.

That matters because militaries, including Ukraine’s, increasingly rely on commercial satellites for communications and imagery.

In October 2022, a senior Russian foreign ministry official told the United Nations that “quasi-civilian infrastructure may be a legitimate target for a retaliatory strike”.

Juliana Suess, a space security researcher at the German Institute for International and Security Affairs (SWP) in Berlin, said Russia may be calculating that reactions will be less severe if it shadows a commercial satellite rather than a sovereign one, especially one not belonging to the US.

ICEYE-X36 is owned by ICEYE’s US subsidiary and registered as a US satellite, Hilborne noted, adding, “this creates a complex problem”.

The distance matters too. A gap of less than 5km may sound far, Suess said, but “it’s essentially a hop and a skip in space”.

“It’s incredibly close and could potentially enable Russia to conduct nefarious activity, including intercepting data from the satellite or disrupting its service – temporarily via signal jamming, for example,” she added.

“A kinetic attack would also be possible but seems less likely at this point in time, in part because this would be an unprecedented measure taken against a satellite”, she explained.

Is Russia just sending a message, or escalating?

“It is sending a message that these platforms could be held under threat,” Hilborne said, adding that it also represents an escalation, suggesting Russia might be willing to attack, since any satellite could be used as a weapon simply by crashing it into another.

Suess added: “I think regardless of whether we see further manoeuvring or consequences, the political goal of intimidation should not be underestimated”.

“The manoeuvre is also a message that space assets cannot be considered wholly safe or removed from the war in Ukraine”, she said.

She pointed to November 2021, when Russia destroyed one of its own satellites with a missile, an event referred to in the European Union’s 2023 space strategy.

“We have long known what Russia is capable of in terms of disrupting or even destroying space assets. This manoeuvre is also a reminder of those previously demonstrated capabilities,” she said.

Moscow calls such spacecraft “inspector satellites”, and in 2020 described such manoeuvres as common practice “by many countries”, Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty reported.

Hilborne described the approach as “another example of activity that sits below the threshold of conflict”.

An outright attack on ICEYE-X36 looks unlikely for now, Hilborne said.

“With the current balance in the conflict, and this being an American-registered satellite, it would seem unlikely that Russia would actually attack the satellite, as the response would be unpredictable”, he said.

An attack could also create a large amount of space debris, which would be a problem for everyone, he added, warning that “it’s hard to second-guess where Russia draws the line”.

How has Ukraine fought to keep its eyes in space?

Ukraine’s access to satellites has come under pressure before, at times from its own allies.

In March 2025, as Washington paused intelligence sharing with Kyiv, the US National Geospatial-Intelligence Agency “temporarily suspended” Ukraine’s access to the main portal for US government-purchased commercial imagery.

If ICEYE-X36 were disrupted, Ukraine would not necessarily go blind, Suess said, because the ICEYE constellation has more than one satellite, and sovereign radar satellites, such as Germany’s, could also provide data.

But speed is the issue. According to ICEYE, the expanded access agreed this year meant faster access, Suess explained.

“The question is whether a similarly fast transfer of data could be enabled with a new provider, whether commercial or sovereign in nature,” she said.

Now, Ukraine faces another squeeze. Last week, the order to limit Starshield – the military-grade version of SpaceX’s Starlink service – for Ukraine came from inside the White House, two US officials and a Western official told Reuters.

On Saturday, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Starshield is currently unavailable to Ukraine, but that Kyiv’s request to use it for attacks deep inside Russia is “under discussion”.

articles.title: Daniel Rotman spotted a gap in the cat-litter market and built PrettyLitter; Mars later bought out his stake at a reported $1.4 billion valuation
articles.summary: Daniel Rotman saw an opportunity in a market he believed had been overlooked: cat care.
articles.body: Daniel Rotman saw an opportunity in a market he believed had been overlooked: cat care. In 2015, after an experience that left him questioning how early cat owners could spot signs of illness, he began exploring whether cat litter could do more than absorb waste. The result was PrettyLitter, a colour-changing silica gel litter designed to alert owners to potential changes in their cats’ urine. Rotman built the business by selling directly to consumers, handling early orders himself and prioritising profitability over rapid hiring. He reported generating about $760,000 in revenue in the first year. Bloomberg reported in September 2021 that Mars had agreed to acquire PrettyLitter in a deal valued at $500 million to $1 billion, citing people familiar with the matter. In June 2026, Inc. reported that Mars took a majority stake in the company in 2021 and bought out Daniel Rotman’s equity in 2024 at a reported $1.4 billion valuation.How Daniel Rotman’s experience with his cat inspired PrettyLitterThe idea behind PrettyLitter came from the loss of Rotman’s 15-year-old cat, Gingi. In his first-person account published by Entrepreneur, Rotman recalled that his cat’s health deteriorated after she had appeared to behave normally. A veterinarian explained that cats often hide signs of illness, making changes difficult for owners to notice early. A few years later, in 2015, Rotman was participating in an incubator programme and revisited the experience. He wondered whether the litter box, which cat owners use every day, could provide an early indication of potential health concerns. He also recalled learning from the veterinarian that urine testing can help identify health problems in cats and dogs.At the time, Rotman had completed graduate school and was considering a career in public policy. The incubator gave him an opportunity to develop the idea into a business concept. He researched veterinary laboratories and found one that helped formulate the product. PrettyLitter was designed to change colour in response to certain characteristics of a cat’s urine. Rotman has stressed that the product is not a diagnostic tool. Instead, it is intended to alert owners to potential changes that may warrant veterinary attention. A colour change cannot establish that an animal has a particular illness, and owners should consult a veterinarian about concerning results or changes in behaviour.How PrettyLitter works and how Rotman funded the businessRotman selected type C silica gel as the product’s base material. In his Entrepreneur account, he said the material’s properties helped the company develop a litter that could absorb urine while displaying colour changes associated with certain urine conditions. Unlike conventional clumping litter, PrettyLitter absorbs moisture into its pores rather than forming clumps that must be scooped out after every use. Rotman said the material also required less product by weight, helping make shipping more practical. The early business operated on a small scale. Rotman learned to use Shopify and Facebook advertising, packed orders in his apartment and took parcels to the post office himself. According to his account, the operation outgrew his bedroom within about six months, prompting him to move fulfilment to an external facility. Rotman reported generating approximately $760,000 in revenue during the first year, followed by $6.5 million in the second year. Inc. also reported revenue of about $750,000 in 2016 and $6.5 million in 2017, broadly corroborating the figures for those years.The company’s early funding also needs to be distinguished from its later seed round. According to Inc.’s June 2026 profile, PrettyLitter placed third in Draper University’s Startup U competition, after which venture capitalist Tim Draper invested $50,000. Rotman’s account in Entrepreneur differs: he says his pitch won the consumer-facing category and earned him a $50,000 cheque. The two accounts differ on the competition result and how the money was awarded. PrettyLitter subsequently raised a $1 million seed round, which closed in November 2016, according to Inc. Rotman said he focused on profitability, gross margins and keeping the business lean rather than expanding its headcount simply to signal growth. He initially outsourced work and hired employees as specific operational needs arose. His first hire was a customer-service director, after the volume of customer enquiries became difficult to manage alone.Mars acquisition: what is known about PrettyLitter’s valuationAs PrettyLitter grew, the cost of manufacturing inventory ahead of customer payments created a financing challenge. Rotman explained that he had to consider taking on debt or finding a strategic partner who could help fund the next stage of growth. He had maintained relationships with people at Mars, the privately held multinational behind a range of food and pet-care businesses. Rotman described the conversation as a strategic discussion, while Inc. reported that the process developed into a competitive bidding process. In September 2021, Bloomberg reported that Mars had agreed to acquire PrettyLitter in a deal valued at $500 million to $1 billion, citing people familiar with the matter. Mars declined to comment on the price, according to the report.More recent reporting adds an important distinction. In a June 12, 2026, article, Inc. reported that Mars bought a majority stake in PrettyLitter in 2021 in a mid-nine-figure transaction, then bought out Rotman’s equity in 2024 at a reported $1.4 billion valuation. Inc. reported that PrettyLitter had around $115 million in annual revenue and 12 full-time employees at the time of the 2021 acquisition. Rotman’s account in Entrepreneur lists revenue figures of $125 million, $250 million and $350 million, but does not date those figures. The two accounts therefore report different revenue figures, and the timing of the figures in Rotman’s account is not specified. Rotman said Mars appealed to him because of its experience in pet care and veterinary services, its long-term ownership structure and its ability to provide resources for product development. articles.title: Israeli attacks kill at least four Palestinians in Gaza
articles.summary: A couple and a 17-year-old are among those killed by Israeli air attacks and gunfire in the Gaza Strip.
articles.body:
At least four Palestinians, including a couple and a 17-year-old, have been killed in Israeli air attacks and gunfire in separate incidents in the Gaza Strip, health officials said.

An Israeli air strike killed Akram Yassin and his wife Dina Abu Baker in an apartment in Gaza City, medics said on Tuesday.

In Khan Younis, in southern Gaza, a 17-year-old boy was killed by Israeli gunfire near the Qizan an-Najjar neighbourhood. Another person was killed by Israeli gunfire in the Zeitoun suburb east of Gaza City.

The Israeli military also carried out artillery attacks in other areas south of Khan Younis, Palestinian news agency Wafa reported.

Al Jazeera’s Tareq Abu Azzoum, reporting from Deir el-Balah in Gaza, said there has been a surge in Israeli attacks across Gaza overnight and into the early hours of Tuesday.

“We can see that the attacks have been pretty much concentrated on Gaza City, where a residential flat was targeted without any warning,” he said.

“We are seeing very distressing scenes, and footage coming from the site of the attack shows the scale of destruction that has been inflicted upon the whole residential area,” he added.

“We also saw a clear activation of Israeli drones and fighter jets through the early hours of this morning across the central areas of the territory.”

Palestinians inspected the aftermath of the strike on the apartment in Gaza City before gathering for the couple’s funeral.

“We’re supposed to be in a ceasefire period, but honestly, we are not seeing a ceasefire or anything. The war is still going on, assassinations are continuing, and the shelling has not stopped,” Mahmoud Yassin, whose brother was killed, told the Reuters news agency.

Israel’s genocidal war against Palestinians in Gaza has killed at least 74,480 people since October 2023, with another 175,539 wounded, according to the Gaza health authorities.

Since the so-called “ceasefire” in October 2025, 1,522 Palestinians have been killed and 5,421 wounded in Israeli attacks, and 839 bodies have been recovered from under the rubble.

About 82 percent of structures in Gaza, roughly 200,000 buildings, have been damaged, with about two-thirds of them destroyed since the start of the war, according to the United Nations.

articles.title: BBC Scotland TV channel to close amid cuts to services
articles.summary: The station, which started in February 2019, will move to BBC iPlayer in spring next year.
articles.body:
The BBC has announced plans to close its Scotland linear TV station as it seeks to make £500m savings.

The channel, which started in February 2019, will move to BBC iPlayer in spring next year, although its nightly News at Seven programme will close.

The change is expected to see about 10 posts cut in addition to the 60 BBC Scotland announced earlier this year.

Director of BBC Scotland, Hayley Valentine, said: "Against the backdrop of significant financial challenges, we must focus our resources where they will have the greatest impact for audiences."

The BBC said a wide range of its programming currently shown on the linear TV channel would be available online or on BBC One or BBC Two in Scotland.

Shows include Scotland's Home of the Year, Murder Case, Inside Barlinnie, the Scottish Cup Final and Hogmanay.

The broadcaster's SPFL Championship matches on Friday evenings will move to BBC Two in Scotland.

In other changes, the corporation said BBC Three and Radio Four Extra would be moving online .

A spokesperson for National Union of Journalists (NUJ) said it has asked the UK chancellor to intervene urgently to "prevent further damaging cuts" and called on BBC management to find alternative savings.

The spokesperson added: "These are worrying proposals for the future of public service broadcasting in Scotland, and would see fewer journalists producing less news at a time when quality trusted news is needed more than ever."

Scotland's Culture Secretary Màiri McAllan said the Scottish government strongly opposed the "wholly unacceptable" proposals.

She added: "This represents a significant blow to our media landscape and is the latest example of a long-standing pattern of BBC underinvestment in Scotland, raising serious questions about the broadcaster's commitment to Scottish audiences and the creative sector, and its public service obligations to serve all parts of the UK fairly and equitably."

Last month, new BBC Director General Matt Brittin said given current finances and changing audience habits it "may well mean" some channels and radio stations close so resources can be invested in on-demand services.

Brittin told BBC One's Sunday With Laura Kuenssberg that "we wouldn't guarantee any programme or any channel will exist forever".

The BBC previously announced it would cut between 1,800 and 2,000 - almost one in 10 jobs - as part of measures to make £500m savings in the next two years.

In June, 550 job cuts were announced in news, nations and TV and radio content as part of its first stage of cuts.

In recent months, the BBC announced a series of closures of programmes including Blankety Blank, Celebrity Mastermind, Live At The Apollo and Football Focus. Cuts to radio programmes have also been announced.

The broadcaster, which has about 21,500 full time employees, gets most of its income from the licence fee, but the number of TV licences sold has been declining in recent years.

Plans for a dedicated BBC Scotland TV channel were announced in 2017 by then BBC Director General Tony Hall.

He said the "bold, creative and ambitious" channel would replace BBC Two Scotland as the main home for Scottish-produced programmes.

It gained Ofcom approval and was launched in February 2019 with the investment of 80 journalism jobs.

It was fronted by flagship news programme The Nine which covered Scottish, UK and international stories from a Scottish perspective.

The channel also became home to Scottish drama, comedy, documentaries, current affairs and sport including Debate Night and Scottish national team football games.

In 2024, five years after it went on air, the BBC announced plans to scrap The Nine alongside entertainment news show The Edit and weekly news review Seven Days.

It was replaced by a shorter 30-minute news programme News at Seven, as well as extended versions of Reporting Scotland.

'Extremely proud of the News at Seven team'

Valentine, who was launch editor of the The Nine, said it was "always sad" to see programmes come to an end.

She praised staff by saying: "I am extremely proud of the News at Seven team and everything they have delivered since launching.

"Our teams are highly skilled, and we will continue to evolve our news and current affairs offer to reflect the changing way people consume journalism today."

Valentine added that by "continuing the channel on BBC iPlayer, we can ensure Scottish content thrives in a digital environment".

"BBC Two in Scotland, alongside BBC One Scotland, will maintain a strong and distinctive Scottish presence on linear television," she said.

BBC Scotland's Head of News Howard Simpson said: "Losing one of our programme brands is hard.

"Reporting Scotland: News at Seven succeeds in bringing our audience closer to the day's news and has been incredibly effective at adding context from experts and from a first-person experience.

"The team who work on the show bring energy and creativity and a fresh look at our TV offer. I am extremely proud of what they continue to accomplish."

BBC Director General Brittin told staff on Tuesday: "We need to make every pound work harder for audiences as we respond to the immediate cost pressures and reinvent the BBC for a changing world. We all know that means tough choices."

articles.title: UWE Bristol student murdered housemate by stabbing him 30 times
articles.summary: Jamie Collins is described as a "sensitive and caring young man" after his killer admits murder.
articles.body:
A student who stabbed his housemate more than 30 times in a masked ambush has changed his murder plea to guilty.

Zack Coughlan, 23, attacked Jamie Collins, 21, in an alleyway near the garden of their home on 8 April and then left his body outside for eight hours before calling police.

A murder trial had been under way at Bristol Crown Court because Coughlan initially denied the charge, although he did admit killing Collins. He told jurors he stabbed Collins because he feared his housemate would kill him .

However, Coughlan, of Cleve Road, Filton, has now changed his plea to guilty and will be sentenced for murder on Wednesday.

Describing him as "a sensitive and caring young man", Collins' family said he had been "looking forward to finishing his journey" at the University of the West of England (UWE) and returning home to Swansea "in a matter of weeks".

"His passion for equality stood out to everyone who knew him. His unapologetic inclusivity will be his legacy for all of us. We know he was heading for a hugely successful future following his engineering and robotics degree," they added.

The men were both final-year robotics students at the UWE and lived together in a house in Filton, owned by Coughlan.

During the trial, Coughlan claimed he was fearful of Collins , telling jurors he was "barely able to think" when he lay in wait for his housemate to return from university before stabbing him repeatedly.

Coughlan then left his housemate to die in the alleyway behind their home before cycling away on the victim's bike to dispose of bloodstained evidence.

He dumped the bike at a nearby retail park, bought a change of clothes and threw his bloodstained clothing in a pond, in carrier bags weighed down with bricks.

On returning home he ate pizza and played video games, claiming he "had to disconnect" from what happened. He did not call 999 for another five hours.

The entire attack was caught on CCTV Coughlan had installed himself, which also captures the moment he staged the discovery of Collins' body.

Jurors were told he later rewatched this footage five times.

Det Ch Insp Lucy Edgeworth, of the major crime investigation team, said "all the evidence suggests" the killing was a "pre-planned, cold-blooded execution".

She said despite Coughlan claiming his housemate's political views had become more extreme and that he had talked about killing Coughlan, the motive for the murder was "not clear".

"We know there was a dispute about rent. We know that they held different political views. But none of those things make any sense to why somebody would carry out such a horrific crime," she said.

Edgeworth pointed out inconsistencies in Coughlan's story, including claims he had injured his hands climbing a tree after the incident, which she called "slightly odd".

She added the defendant's blood had been found on Collins' recovered bike because he had likely injured himself in the "ferocious and horrendous" attack.

"The retrieval of the clothing from the pond, again, all forensically linked Zach to that crime. So it was a really interesting and complex forensic picture," she said.

In a statement issued outside court, surrounded by Collins' family, Edgeworth described the murder as "meticulously planned".

"The brutal nature of what he did cannot be underestimated," she said.

"Rather than calling for medical help he did everything to protect himself.

"He feigned shock and the lies continued, both to police and friends in the hours and days after what happened."

Coughlan changed his plea to guilty after a legal ruling by the trial judge on Tuesday.

Judge Justice Linden said Coughlan's partial defence of manslaughter by reason of loss of control could not be left to the jury to consider as part of their deliberations on the murder charge.

He told the jury: "You will have just heard that the defendant has changed his plea to the indictment to guilty.

"That means that he now admits the charge of murder.

"I would like, on behalf of us all, to thank you for the service that you have given in this case."

In a statement issued following the verdict, Collins' family said his death had affected them in a "deep, profound and lasting way".

They said: "As a family we have had to explain repeatedly to people what has happened.

"Every time we do so it reinforces the pain of him having been killed so suddenly, and in such a senseless and brutal way.

"Our family has been sickened that Zack Coughlan pretended to help Jamie when in fact he is responsible for killing him."

They added he had accumulated enough points during his studies that he was posthumously awarded a 2:1 degree in July, which the family accepted on his behalf.

The university described him as a "valued member" of the robotics community and an active member of student societies.

"He was a natural engineer, keen in robotics, a hard worker and only weeks away from completing his degree," said UWE Bristol vice-chancellor Steve West.

"The details which have emerged during the trial are shocking, and particularly difficult for several of his university friends who were called as witnesses.

"The number of friends and university staff who attended both Jamie's memorial and the court trial is testament to how much he was cared for."

articles.title: Royals roll out the red carpet in Windsor for visiting Sultan
articles.summary: The Sultan of Oman, leader of a Middle Eastern strategic partner, is welcomed to Windsor for a state visit.
articles.body:
The King and Queen, along with the Prince and Princess of Wales, were part of a colourful ceremonial welcome for the Sultan of Oman as his state visit to the UK begins.

The red carpet was rolled out in Windsor for the ruler of Oman, which is an important strategic partner in the Middle East against the backdrop of the conflict with Iran.

It has been seen as a diplomatic bridge between the West and Iran and Sultan Haitham bin Tarik Al Said will be given the full soft power treatment from his royal hosts.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham will join the Omani visitors at a spectacular state banquet on Tuesday evening, ahead of political discussions at Downing Street on Wednesday.

Prince William greeted the Sultan on Tuesday morning, the pair sheltering under umbrellas.

Waiting to formally welcome the Omani delegation were the King and Queen and the Princess of Wales, before they all travelled in a carriage ride to Windsor Castle.

State visits are a mix of pageantry and politics, with the carefully choreographed hospitality providing an opportunity for talks about important strategic alliances and to promote military and business links.

This visit is taking place against the sensitive background of tensions in the Middle East, with Oman facing Iran, on the other side of the strategically important Strait of Hormuz and the Gulf of Oman.

Tuesday evening will see Burnham's first state banquet since becoming prime minister. He will take one of the places of honour in St George's Hall, on a lavishly decorated table that can seat about 160 guests.

Burnham previously spoke to the Sultan in July, when they discussed efforts to open the Strait of Hormuz to shipping, and the prime minister said he was grateful for Oman's attempts at mediation.

The guest list does not include non-working royals, like the Duke and Duchess of Sussex.

An interview with Prince Harry with GQ was released as the state visit was getting under way.

He talked about his complicated relationship with his father and brother - recognising that it was something that was "massively relatable" for the public.

"Some people don't want it to work out," he said. "I want it to work out.

"With everything else that's going on in the world, the most important thing is to reconcile - that's the key point... scars stick around forever."

In the interview, which took place in New York, he said he would "encourage everybody" to let go of the past.

"If there's certain things from the past that are still affecting you every day, that's harder to let go of," he told GQ.

"But, for me, there's enough drama in the world and enough drama in people's lives to continue with issues with family."

articles.title: Look of the Week: Jenna Ortega’s steel dress has a very human touch
articles.summary: The Elias Matso gown was painstakingly crafted from steel flat and spiral boning — components usually found in the guts of a corset or hoop skirt.
articles.body: From a certain handmade $50 million white-gold bra to the latest red carpet look worn by Jenna Ortega, metal couture is everywhere this week. At first glance, Ortega’s fitted bodice, fringe skirt and W-shaped bustier looked like something you might find hanging in Cher’s closet. But the gown, designed by Elias Matso, was fashioned almost entirely out of hand-cut steel flat and spiral boning — structural components usually found in the guts of a corset or hoop skirt. It looked as if Ortega herself had been magnetized and sent naked into a steel factory. She wore the dress to the New York film premiere of “Klara and the Sun,” an adaptation of Kazuo Ishiguro’s 2021 novel by the same name. In it, Ortega plays an eager and altruistic solar-powered robot, or “Artificial Friend” called Klara. “He’s been holding onto this dress for me and it’s perfect,” Ortega told People magazine of Matso’s design. “It’s very fitting for the film.” Ortega and her stylist, Enrique Melendez, would have had plenty of options to choose from for this method dressing moment. Luxury fashion — an industry that justifies its price tag through the promise of human craftsmanship — has enjoyed nodding to robots, and in particular fem-bots, for decades. There was Thierry Mugler’s Machinemensch suit from 1995, recently brought out of retirement by Zendaya, named after the revolutionary sculpted robot costume Brigitte Helm wears in Fritz Lang’s seminal 1927 movie “Metropolis.” In 2024, Schiaparelli’s spring couture collection used technological waste salvaged from the 2000’s, from discarded circuit boards to Nokia cell phones. Creative director Daniel Roseberry cheekily likened the electronics to “vintage fabrics.” And then there was the landmark spring 1999 Alexander McQueen show, where automated robotic arms spray-painted model Shalom Harlow’s white dress into oblivion. Today, tech-fashion is a much more sobering prospect than a fantasy robot suit with exposed butt checks. Meta has collaborated with Kylie Jenner and Ray-Ban to make their controversial AI glasses more aesthetically pleasing, and real robots are closer than ever before to the world of fashion. This summer, Unitree Robotics’ humanoid dancers were meme-ified a million times over when they performed at Vogue World in Milan, with designers such as Miuccia Prada and Alessandro Michele looking particularly disgruntled in the front row. At Shangai Fashion Week earlier this month, Unitree’s robots showed up again — this time modeling wedding dresses on the runway for Chinese brand The Atelier. For it to work, or at least entice rather than unnerve, tech-fashion has to have an analog element. Roseberry repurposed the outdated materials of an early aughts IT department, while McQueen’s robotic arms were borrowed from a factory where they were used to paint cars — hardly super high-tech advancements threatening species-level extinction. Matso’s gown, too, though resembling a motherboard’s insides, was just dressmaker’s metal. Both the designer and Ortega emphasized the people that put it all together. Matso nodded to the “many blisters, rebuilds, failed trials” and “helping hands.” Ortega put it more simply: “It’s hand-made, human-made, a lot of effort.”

articles.title: Jon Stewart: Trump waiving Russia sanctions ‘insane’ and ‘incoherent’
articles.summary: Jon Stewart blasted President Trump for waiving sanctions on Russia to allow more of its diesel to come to market, calling the move “insane” and “incoherent.” The president signed an executive order last week that waived the sanctions bill he signed into law in September. The legislative package, which was passed by Congress with bipartisan…
articles.body:
Jon Stewart blasted President Trump for waiving sanctions on Russia to allow more of its diesel to come to market, calling the move “insane” and “incoherent.”

The president signed an executive order last week that waived the sanctions bill he signed into law in September. The legislative package, which was passed by Congress with bipartisan support and named after the late Sen. Lindsey Graham (R-S.C.), would have imposed tariffs on top Russian energy purchasers and other countries helping Moscow to evade sanctions.

The bill’s supporters had said its aim was to target resources needed by Russia in its continued war against Ukraine.

Earlier this month, Trump announced a deal he said he struck with Russian President Vladimir Putin for Russia to “immediately” supply 300,000 tons of diesel to the U.S. and the global marketplace.

“Why would we motivate a group to sell diesel when we just put sanctions on them for selling diesel?” Stewart asked as he hosted Monday’s “Daily Show” on Comedy Central.

“Doing the opposite within a month is insane,” Stewart exclaimed.

“It is illogical. It is incoherent,” the comedian said.

Responding to comments made in a recent CNN interview by Energy Secretary Chris Wright defending Trump’s move and saying, “This is pressuring Russia,” Stewart said, “By giving them money? How is this punishing Russia?”

Stewart unveiled a prop, a set of Russian matryoshka dolls, to provide what he called “a physical demonstration of the many layers of stupidity that must be behind this decision.”

In response to additional comments by Wright backing the president, Stewart opened up one of the dolls to reveal a smaller one inside.

“I think I might’ve discovered the real reason,” Stewart said, as he opened the smallest of the nesting dolls to reveal a tiny photo of Trump and Putin standing side by side.
