articles.title: BBC closures make business sense, but far more savings are needed, says Katie Razzall
articles.summary: The BBC announced it will close its BBC Three, BBC Scotland and Radio 4 Extra broadcast channels.
articles.body:
The BBC's announcement that it will close three of its linear broadcast channels - BBC Three, BBC Scotland and Radio 4 Extra - makes sense financially.

BBC Three's most popular show on Monday night was a repeat of an old episode of Top Gear. Around 77,000 people tuned in.

BBC Scotland's TV channel was watched, according to this year's annual report, by a weekly average of 12% of the Scottish population. Scots simply aren't tuning in in the numbers to make it cost-effective.

(Fascinatingly, BBC Alba, which is aimed at Gaelic speakers and learners, reached 43% of Scots weekly - was it boosted by its rights to broadcast Italian football's Serie A, with the commentary mainly in Gaelic?)

It's hard to argue - although no doubt some will - that there is a business case for keeping BBC Scotland's TV channel open.

The same goes for BBC Three, although the hokey cokey that has gone on with that channel - launched to fanfare in 2003, later made digital-only, then brought back to linear in 2022, now back online only again - has looked indecisive. Bizarre even.

But the bigger picture is that viewers and listeners are already migrating online - increasingly finding the BBC's programmes not via those linear TV and radio channels but on iPlayer, BBC Sounds, and, more recently, YouTube.

So that's the business case - and the BBC needs to save £500m over the next three years. That figure is concentrating minds.

But axing the three linear channels is a drop in the ocean financially. I understand it will save less than £10m in total per year.

Last year the BBC spent £42m creating content for BBC Scotland. It still plans to create many of those shows for iPlayer - and BBC Two in Scotland will be reconfigured to deliver Scotland-only programming.

The part of BBC Three that commissions programmes will actually get more money to spend on creating content aimed specifically at 16-34s (with a core focus on the 16-25s).

This was the network that commissioned Normal People, Fleabag, Killing Eve - programmes of quality and wide appeal.

There's also been a recent announcement of commissions dreamt up specifically for YouTube - to reach those 16-24s who the BBC (and other public service broadcasters) find so difficult to lure to their own platforms.

Many of Radio 4 Extra's programmes will also still be on BBC Sounds. If you listen to the Daily Service, first broadcast in 1928 and the longest-running programme of its kind anywhere in the world, you will still be able to find it.

So these aren't major cost savings. The BBC would likely argue, when it comes to audiences, who are at the heart of everything, it is pivoting to find them where they already are.

What's been announced today is more about the direction of travel. It's about the continuing evolution of the BBC, a streamlining as audience habits change.

That doesn't mean it isn't painful to all of us inside the BBC. Job cuts are always difficult. In News, 100 more roles are being axed. That's on top of the 200 already announced. And the news division is still nowhere near its target of £51m of cuts.

And with only two fifths of the £500m of total savings now announced, there is still a very long way to go.

As a BBC user, you are going to hear much more about cuts in the coming months. Some will think that is a good thing as the BBC reflects the belt-tightening going on in most homes and companies across the UK. Others fear that the BBC's important role in public life is being chipped away.

There is a bigger fight going on here. The BBC is negotiating with the government over its future - and how it will be paid for. It won't harm the negotiations if it can show the corporation is being streamlined and made more efficient.

As long as it can also demonstrate that audiences aren't being left behind.

articles.title: Bela Bajaria’s season finale: Desi content queen exits Netflix
articles.summary: TOI Correspondent from Washington: Bela Bajaria's rise from her family's car-wash business to the top of Netflix was a classic immigrant success story.
articles.body: TOI Correspondent from Washington: Bela Bajaria's rise from her family's car-wash business to the top of Netflix was a classic immigrant success story. As chief content officer at the streaming giant, she knew how to keep millions of viewers eating up hours binge-watching. Keeping her own job, it turns out, was a series she couldn't renew.Word in the industry is that Netflix has shown the door to the desi content queen, who oversaw an annual budget of close to $ 20 billion and turned the streaming platform into a global television powerhouse. The exit comes as Netflix faces mounting pressure to deliver bigger hits and keep viewers hooked. She is being replaced by former Disney and Fox executive Peter Rice in a shake-up that comes amid layoffs affecting about 1,000 employees, or 6% of Netflix's workforce.Netflix has officially described Bajaria's departure as a leadership change, rather than announcing a dismissal, but the timing suggests that its bosses want a reset. Audience engagement has slowed, the company has struggled to reproduce the cultural impact of some of its biggest hits, and investors are scrutinising how effectively its vast content spending translates into viewing.Netflix boss Ted Sarandos, who once credited Bajaria with transforming its global content operation, has indicated that the company wants to take its programming slate to the next level, particularly in the US and Canada. According to a report in the WSJ, he has been complaining internally for months that Americans are spending less time watching Netflix and the service was short on new hit shows.Bajaria's own journey has been remarkable and worthy of a show. Born in London in 1970 to Indian parents, she moved to the US as a child and worked in her family's car-wash business before entering television as an assistant at CBS in 1996. She rose through CBS and NBCUniversal, eventually becoming president of Universal Television -- the first Indian to head a major studio -- where she oversaw productions including Brooklyn Nine-Nine, The Mindy Project and Unbreakable Kimmy Schmidt.She joined Netflix in 2016, initially handling licensing, co-productions and unscripted programming, before becoming head of global television in 2020 and chief content officer in January 2023. Her tenure coincided with global hits including Squid Game, Bridgerton, Beef, Adolescence, Lupin, Cobra Kai, KPop Demon Hunters, and Frankenstein, alongside reality programming and Netflix's expansion into live events and sports.For India, her contribution went beyond having a desi face in Hollywood's executive suite. She championed the idea that distinctly local stories could travel globally, helping expand Netflix's Indian-language ambitions. Indian Matchmaking generated worldwide discussion, while Delhi Crime, Mismatched and films such as Amar Singh Chamkila helped diversify the platform's Indian offering. articles.title: Elderly couple plead not guilty to shooting son-in-law to death at California park
articles.summary: The elderly couple accused of killing their son-in-law, New York Times executive Jonathan McKinsey, pleaded not guilty to first-degree murder with a special circumstance of lying in wait, a defense attorney said Monday.
articles.body: The elderly couple accused of killing their son-in-law, New York Times executive Jonathan McKinsey, pleaded not guilty to first-degree murder with a special circumstance of lying in wait, a defense attorney said Monday. Defense attorney Curtis Briggs argued that his client, Shili Chen, who is married to Shouyong Zhang, did not premeditate the shooting, NBC Bay Area reported. Instead, Briggs told NBC Bay Area that the couple, both 77, acted out of concern after seeing something disturbing while their son-in-law had a supervised visit with his children. “My client was absolutely concerned for her own life and also concerned for her grandchildren,” Briggs told NBC Bay Area. Zhang is being represented by a public defender. Alameda County prosecutors say Chen and Zhang watched and waited in a parking lot in Dublin, California, to attack McKinsey, who was embroiled in a bitter divorce and custody battle with their daughter. Briggs said that McKinsey, 40, had previously threatened Chen’s life three times through a hit man. The couple purchased firearms in March to defend themselves, Briggs said, and were moved to act last month in the parking lot of a popular park. “They are not cold-blooded killers. They didn’t premeditate anything,” Briggs told NBC Bay Area. Briggs did not elaborate on what the elderly couple witnessed that drove them to kill their son-in-law. If convicted, they could both face life in prison without the possibility of parole. According to local police, 911 calls started coming in around 3 p.m. on Sept. 26 from terrified witnesses, many of whom were with their young children. Several witnesses told police they saw a black Honda speeding out of the parking lot and later identified Chen and Zhang as the shooters, police said in a statement. Officers chased down the car and arrested the couple, according to the police report. Nearly a decade’s worth of court documents revealed a deeply troubled marriage between McKinsey and his wife, Candice Jang, who has not been charged in connection with his death. McKinsey’s death followed years of violent struggle between Jang and McKinsey, who started dating in 2008 and were married in 2011, according to Jang’s petition for a domestic abuse restraining order. They had three children. McKinsey had recently filed for divorce and was scheduled to appear in court the same week he died, according to court records. In separate petitions for restraining orders, McKinsey and Jang each argued that the other was physically and mentally abusive during their marriage. McKinsey and Jang both said they wanted full custody of their children, but McKinsey had an ongoing child abuse case that granted him only supervised visits. The children were living with Jang and her parents when McKinsey was shot. He had been previously charged with two misdemeanors — cruelty to a child by endangering health and corporal injury to a child. McKinsey was freed on $50,000 bail and had been trying to enter a mental health diversion program, according to court records. Had he successfully completed the program, the charges would have been dismissed. According to police reports, Zhang admitted to shooting McKinsey with his firearm during interviews with investigators. The husband and wife were each carrying weapons at the time of their arrests. “Chen and the passenger carried out this shooting in a crowded park parking lot with blatant disregard for public safety where several children were present,” the arresting officer said. McKinsey allegedly threatened to kill Chen at least three times, NBC Bay Area reported. A bail hearing was set for Nov. 4, followed by a pretrial hearing on Nov. 23.

articles.title: Bannon ‘not wild’ about Trump endorsing Netanyahu
articles.summary: Former White House adviser Steve Bannon on Monday said he’s “not wild” about President Trump endorsing Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu ahead of Israel’s election next week. articles.body:
Former White House adviser Steve Bannon on Monday said he’s “not wild” about President Trump endorsing Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu ahead of Israel’s election next week.

Trump on Sunday called the prime minister “Strong, Brave, and Brilliant in the face of tremendous opposition, including that coming from even Israel, itself,” adding that he represents “the kind of Partner that the United States of America is demanding of Israel.”

“An endorsement by President Trump that, as you can imagine, in the War Room, we were not wild about,” Bannon said on his “War Room” podcast. “He endorsed wholeheartedly Netanyahu over the weekend, and I take a very different take on Netanyahu. One of the things we’ve been pushing here is: where is the investigation of the Oct. 7 situation?”

Bannon referred to reporting by former Jerusalem Post editor-in-chief Yaakov Katz that accused Israel’s government of failing to respond to intelligence indicating Hamas would attack on Oct. 7, 2023. The subsequent attack killed around 1,200 Israelis and led to the country’s yearslong assault on the Gaza Strip.

“But as I said at the time, I said, ‘This thing’s so disturbing, when are we going to see an actual investigation by the Israeli government, or Israeli citizens with the government, or however you want to do it?'” Bannon continued.

He accused Netanyahu’s government of not allowing an investigation and said the U.S. should launch “a massive investigation of our own” into the events leading up to the Oct. 7 attack.

The New York Times and Israeli news outlet Haaretz reported last month that the Emirati President Sheikh Mohammed Bin Zayed warned Netanyahu about a possible major attack on Israel before October 2023. Netanyahu denied Haaretz’s reporting and vowed on the social platform X to sue the outlet for “a malicious fabrication with clear political timing.”

Israel and Hamas agreed to a ceasefire last October, but Israeli military strikes since the ceasefire have led to more Palestinians deaths in the last year. More than 74,000 Palestinians in Gaza have died since the start of the war, including after the ceasefire, according to the Hamas-led Gaza Ministry of Health.

Netanyahu is seeking an unprecedented seventh term as Israel’s prime minister, having served nonconsecutive terms as the country’s leader since 1996.

He has also faced allegations of corruption and was indicted on fraud and bribery charges in 2019, which has since gone to trial. The International Criminal Court issued an arrest warrant for Netanyahu, accusing him, Hamas leader Mohammed Diab Ibrahim Al-Masri and former Israeli Defense Minister Yoav Gallant of committing war crimes and crimes against humanity during the war in Gaza.

Netanyahu has denied the charges in connection with the corruption trial and has denied allegations made over his handling of the Israel-Hamas war.

articles.title: Two men re-arrested in RAF Fairford investigation
articles.summary: Counter-terror police say the men have been arrested on suspicion of assisting a foreign intelligence service.
articles.body:
Two men have been re-arrested after an incident near RAF Fairford last month, counter-terrorism police have said.

A 24-year-old UK national, and a 25-year-old dual UK-Iranian national, are being held on suspicion of assisting a foreign intelligence service under Section 3 of the National Security Act 2023, with police saying the investigation relates to Iran.

Police had been alerted to three suspicious vehicles near the US airbase in Gloucestershire in the early hours of 27 September - a major incident was subsequently declared and dozens of homes evacuated.

Seven men had initially been arrested as part of the counter-terror police investigation and were later released on bail.

Five men were found with petrol in three vans near the airbase - they were initially arrested on suspicion of committing offences under the Explosives Act and then further arrested on suspicion of preparation of a terrorist act.

The re-arrests announced on Tuesday relate to a 24-year-old man who was initially held on the 27 September near the base and a 25-year-old who was arrested on suspicion of preparation of terrorist acts days later on 1 October in Westminster.

The other five men remain on police bail.

The head of National Counter Terrorism Policing, Assistant Commissioner Laurence Taylor said: "This is very much a live investigation, and our evidence gathering continues, but at this time our position remains the same; we consider it highly likely that there is Iranian state involvement.

"Our investigators are continuing to examine what that level of involvement was and the ambition behind it."

The officer added that national security investigations can take time to progress due to their sensitive nature.

"Our specialist teams have been working tirelessly to interrogate the many lines of enquiry involved in this hugely complex investigation," he said.

Following the incident, Gloucestershire Police said it had received a call about "three suspicious vehicles" travelling towards RAF Fairford at 00:45 BST.

A bomb disposal team was deployed to the village to examine a number of vehicles, police said at the time.
